finding.claim: deleteAccount never enforces authorization: canDelete(u, a) is called but its boolean result is discarded, so any caller can delete any account by id (broken access control / IDOR).
finding.source: Path parameter id of DELETE /accounts/{id} (per comment at line 19) plus the requesting User u; the User is built by a caller not present in this repo.

trace.note: deleteAccount(User u, long id) receives the request's user and account id
a = accounts.get(id) loads the target account
canDelete(u, a) evaluated but its boolean result is discarded; no throw, no early return

finding.guards_checked: canDelete (lines 9-11) implements admin-or-owner correctly but is not enforced here. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) is the enforcing variant and is used correctly by closeAccount at line 29, but not by deleteAccount. No other guard exists in the file. Exploitability depends on the unseen caller.

verdict.guard_found: canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) is evaluated at line 22 but its boolean is discarded, so it is not effective. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) would throw, but deleteAccount does not call it; closeAccount (line 29) does. No other guard exists in the file.
verdict.reason: Every trace line matches the file: line 22 calls canDelete(u, a) as a bare statement with its result ignored, and line 23 at accounts.remove(id) runs for any caller, while assertCanDelete at lines 13-17 is never used on this path. The only caveat is that the User is built by a caller outside this repo. The file's own route comment (line 19, DELETE /accounts/{id}) indicates an authenticated user can reach it, so the missing authorization check holds for any non-admin user who is not the owner.

finding.claim: Missing and forbidden accounts produce different exceptions (NullPointerException vs SecurityException), which can let an authenticated non-admin enumerate valid account ids if error responses are surfaced to the client.
finding.source: Path parameter id (AccountService.java:19 and :26 comments) supplied by the requesting user.
finding.sink: Observable error response distinguishing nonexistent from existing-but-forbidden account ids (information disclosure); the NPE dereference is at line 10.

trace.note: deleteAccount: a = accounts.get(id) returns null when id does not exist
canDelete(u, a) invoked with a == null
for non-admin u, a.ownerId() dereferences null and throws NullPointerException
closeAccount: same null path via a = accounts.get(id)
for existing foreign account, assertCanDelete throws SecurityException("not allowed"), a different error

finding.guards_checked: No null check on a before canDelete (line 10) or assertCanDelete (line 14). Admin users short-circuit at u.admin() and avoid the NPE. How exceptions are mapped to HTTP responses is not in this repo, so the enumeration impact is unconfirmed. Low severity.

verdict.guard_found: none effective. canDelete (AccountService.java:9-11) returns a bool, but deleteAccount discards it at line 22 as a bare statement, and line 10 dereferences a null account for non-admin callers. assertCanDelete (lines 13-17) throws, but nothing catches it before the effect, and it only runs in closeAccount (line 29). The admin short-circuit at line 10 is not a control against non-admins.
verdict.reason: All trace lines match the code: a null account reaches a.ownerId() at AccountService.java:10 for non-admin users via deleteAccount (lines 21-22) and closeAccount (lines 28-29), while an existing foreign account throws SecurityException at line 15, so the two responses are distinguishable by an authenticated non-admin. The disclosure only reaches the client if the HTTP layer surfaces these exceptions, which is outside this repo. Separately, deleteAccount ignores canDelete's result at line 22 and removes the account at line 23 for any caller, which is a more serious authorization gap than the one claimed.
